Carbohydrates

Structure · Classification · Functions

This lecture covers the biological significance and classification of carbohydrates, the structural forms and isomerism of glucose and other sugars, glycosides, modified monosaccharides, physiologically important disaccharides, storage and structural polysaccharides, and complex carbohydrates (GAGs and glycoproteins).

    Unit index

    Unit 1 of 8

    Biological Significance & Classification

    Core idea: Carbohydrates provide fuel, store energy and help build biological structures; they are classified by the number of sugar units they contain.

    1. Biological Significance of Carbohydrates

    Carbohydrates provide fuel, store energy and help build biological structures. Their biological significance can be grouped into four areas:

    Four areas of significance 4 rows
    AreaSignificance
    1. Structure & metabolismCarbohydrates support cell structures and metabolic processes. Cellulose forms plant cell walls (plant cell: cell wall; animal cell: no cell wall).
    2. Energy / fuelGlucose is a major absorbed sugar and a key fuel for cells; glucose is converted into energy for cells.
    3. Storage & building blocksGlucose is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscle (glycogen storage). Sugars form parts of DNA, RNA and other biomolecules: ribose → RNA; deoxyribose → DNA.
    4. Clinical importanceDiabetes: impaired blood glucose regulation. Lactose intolerance: reduced digestion of lactose.

    Key point. Carbohydrates provide fuel, store energy and help build biological structures.

    2. Classification of Carbohydrates

    Carbohydrates are classified by the number of sugar units they contain (in Figure 1, each bead represents one sugar unit).

    Classes, units, definitions and examples 4 rows
    ClassUnitsDefinition and featuresExamples
    Monosaccharides1Cannot be hydrolyzed into simpler carbohydrates.Glucose, fructose, ribose
    Disaccharides2Two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond.Maltose = glucose + glucose; sucrose = glucose + fructose
    Oligosaccharides3–10Short chains of sugar units. Many resist human digestion and are fermented by gut bacteria.—
    Polysaccharides>10Long chains: linear or branched.Starch, glycogen, cellulose, inulin. Starch is digestible; cellulose is dietary fiber.

    Figure 1. Classification of carbohydrates by the number of sugar units. Panels: Monosaccharide (1 unit) — a single bead; Disaccharide (2 units) — two joined beads; Oligosaccharide (3–10 units) — a short chain of beads; Polysaccharide (>10 units) — a longer chain, linear and branched. Each bead = one sugar unit.

    Subdivisions of monosaccharides 2 ways

    Monosaccharides may be subdivided in two ways. By carbon count: 3 carbons = triose; 4 carbons = tetrose; 5 carbons = pentose; 6 carbons = hexose; 7 carbons = heptose. By functional group: aldose (aldehyde group) and ketose (ketone group).

    Sugar alcohols (polyols) are reduced sugar derivatives, e.g., sorbitol and xylitol; they are used as sweeteners.

    Takeaway. Mono = 1 · Di = 2 · Oligo = 3–10 · Poly = many.

    Quick Review

    • Four areas: structure & metabolism, energy/fuel, storage & building blocks, clinical importance (diabetes, lactose intolerance).
    • Mono = 1 unit (cannot be hydrolyzed) · Di = 2 (glycosidic bond) · Oligo = 3–10 · Poly = >10.
    • Carbon count: triose 3, tetrose 4, pentose 5, hexose 6, heptose 7. Functional group: aldose / ketose.
    • Sugar alcohols (polyols): sorbitol, xylitol — sweeteners.

    Unit 2 of 8

    Structural Forms of Glucose

    Core idea: Glucose can be drawn as an open chain, a flat cyclic ring and a 3D chair; the open-chain and cyclic forms are in equilibrium.

    3. Structural Forms of Glucose

    Glucose can be represented in three ways (Figure 2). (A) The open-chain form, drawn as a Fischer projection, contains an aldehyde group at C1. (B) The cyclic form, drawn as a Haworth projection, is a six-membered ring made of 5 carbons and 1 oxygen. (C) The cyclic form in three dimensions, drawn as a chair conformation, shows the puckered, three-dimensional ring. Panels B and C show the same cyclic molecule from different views; the open-chain and cyclic forms are in equilibrium.

    Figure 2 — three representations 3 panels
    PanelFormDrawing
    AOpen-chain formFischer projection
    BCyclic formHaworth projection
    CCyclic form in 3DChair conformation (α-anomer shown)

    Open-chain glucose (Fischer), carbons 1–6, as drawn in panel A

    CarbonLeftRight
    C1CHO
    C2HOH
    C3HOH
    C4HOH
    C5HOH
    C6CH2OH

    Figure 2. Structural forms of glucose: (A) open-chain Fischer projection; (B) cyclic Haworth projection; (C) cyclic chair conformation (α-anomer shown). In panel B the ring carries HOCH2 on C5, with ring oxygen (O) and carbons numbered 1–5.

    Key point. The cyclic form is thermodynamically favored and predominates.

    Quick Review

    • Three representations: Fischer (open chain, aldehyde at C1) · Haworth (6-membered ring: 5 C + 1 O) · chair (3D).
    • Open-chain ⇌ cyclic equilibrium; the cyclic form is thermodynamically favored and predominates.

    Unit 3 of 8

    Isomerism of Sugars

    Core idea: Five types of isomerism are recognized among sugars: D/L isomers, pyranose/furanose forms, α/β anomers, epimers, and aldose/ketose isomers.

    4. Isomerism of Sugars

    Five types of isomerism are recognized among sugars (Table 1); each is treated in turn below.

    Table 1 — Types of isomerism in sugars 5 rows
    TypeDefinitionExample
    1. D and L isomersMirror-image configurations. In a Fischer projection, the OH on the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl is on the right (D) or left (L).D-glucose and L-glucose
    2. Pyranose and furanose formsPyranose: 6-membered ring (5 carbons + 1 oxygen). Furanose: 5-membered ring (4 carbons + 1 oxygen).Glucopyranose and glucofuranose
    3. Alpha and beta anomersDiffer only at the anomeric carbon.α-D-glucose and β-D-glucose (C1)
    4. EpimersDiffer at only one chiral carbon.Glucose–mannose at C2; glucose–galactose at C4 (D forms)
    5. Aldose and ketose isomersAldose: aldehyde group. Ketose: ketone group.Glucose (aldose) and fructose (ketose), both C6H12O6

    Note. D/L does not indicate optical rotation (+/−).

    4.1 D and L isomerism

    In a Fischer projection, one examines the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl group. For glucose, this is C5, just above CH2OH. If the OH on this carbon lies on the left, the sugar is an L sugar; if it lies on the right, it is a D sugar. L-glucose and D-glucose are mirror images of each other (Figure 3). Most monosaccharides in mammals are D sugars. D/L describes configuration, not the direction of optical rotation.

    Figure 3 — D- and L-glucose (Fischer) 6 carbons
    CarbonL-glucose (left | right)D-glucose (left | right)
    C1CHO (both)
    C2HO | HH | OH
    C3H | OHHO | H
    C4HO | HH | OH
    C5 (reference carbon)HO | H → OH on left → LH | OH → OH on right → D
    C6CH2OH (both)

    Figure 3. D- and L-glucose as Fischer projections, shown as mirror images. The highlighted row is C5, the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl: OH on the left → L sugar; OH on the right → D sugar.

    D/L configuration versus optical rotation

    These are two different properties and must not be confused.

    D or L vs + or − 2 rows
    D or L+ or −
    DescribesArrangement of atomsRotation of light
    How determinedCheck the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl group (Fischer projection, relevant carbon shown, with R above and CH2OH below): OH right → D; OH left → L.Measured experimentally using a polarimeter. Right rotation → (+), dextrorotatory. Left rotation → (−), levorotatory.
    Figure 4 — polarimeter set-up 3 steps
    1. Source of plane-polarized light
    2. Sample tube (with chiral compound)
    3. Analyzer (polarizer)

    Figure 4. Polarimeter set-up: a source of plane-polarized light, a sample tube (with a chiral compound) and an analyzer (polarizer). Measured experimentally using a polarimeter.

    All four combinations are possible: D(+), D(−), L(+) and L(−). For example, D-glucose is D(+) and D-fructose is D(−).

    Key point. D does not mean (+) · L does not mean (−).

    4.2 Pyranose and furanose rings

    A pyranose is a 6-membered ring (5 carbon atoms + 1 oxygen atom), related to the parent ring pyran; a furanose is a 5-membered ring (4 carbon atoms + 1 oxygen atom), related to furan. Examples are α-D-glucopyranose and α-D-glucofuranose (Figure 5). Glucose occurs mainly in the pyranose form.

    Figure 5 — pyranose vs furanose 2 panels
    PyranoseFuranose
    Ring6-membered ring5-membered ring
    Parent ringPyranFuran
    Atoms5 carbon atoms + 1 oxygen atom4 carbon atoms + 1 oxygen atom
    Example shownα-D-Glucopyranoseα-D-Glucofuranose

    Figure 5. Pyranose (6-membered) and furanose (5-membered) rings, with the parent ring systems pyran and furan.

    4.3 Alpha and beta anomers

    Anomers show a different orientation at the anomeric carbon, which in glucose is C1. In α-D-glucopyranose the OH at C1 points down, on the side opposite to CH2OH; in β-D-glucopyranose the OH at C1 points up, on the same side as CH2OH. Anomers differ only at the anomeric carbon. The up/down comparison shown here applies to D-glucose.

    Figure 6 — α- vs β-D-glucopyranose 2 panels
    α-D-Glucopyranoseβ-D-Glucopyranose
    OH at C1Down (opposite side to CH2OH)Up (same side as CH2OH)
    Anomeric carbonC1C1

    Figure 6. α- and β-D-glucopyranose (the C1 hydroxyl is shaded).

    4.4 Epimers

    Epimers are sugars that differ at only one chiral carbon. Relative to α-D-glucose, the reference sugar, α-D-galactose is the C4 epimer and α-D-mannose is the C2 epimer (Figure 7). Only one OH/H arrangement changes. Galactose and mannose differ from each other at two carbons.

    Figure 7 — epimers of glucose 3 sugars
    SugarRelationship to glucose
    α-D-GalactoseC4 epimer of glucose
    α-D-GlucoseReference sugar
    α-D-MannoseC2 epimer of glucose

    Figure 7. Epimers of glucose: galactose (difference at C4) and mannose (difference at C2).

    4.5 Aldose–ketose isomerism

    Aldose and ketose isomers have the same molecular formula (C6H12O6) but a different carbonyl position. D-Glucose is an aldose, with an aldehyde group at C1 (anomeric carbon in the ring: C1). D-Fructose is a ketose, with a ketone group at C2 (anomeric carbon in the ring: C2). Glucose and fructose are structural isomers. Carbonyl groups are shown in the open-chain forms.

    Figure 8 — open-chain D-glucose vs D-fructose 6 carbons
    CarbonD-Glucose — ALDOSE (left | right)D-Fructose — KETOSE (left | right)
    C1CHOCH2OH
    C2H | OHC=O
    C3HO | HHO | H
    C4H | OHH | OH
    C5H | OHH | OH
    C6CH2OHCH2OH
    SummaryAldehyde group at C1 · anomeric carbon in ring: C1Ketone group at C2 · anomeric carbon in ring: C2

    Figure 8. Open-chain forms of D-glucose (aldose) and D-fructose (ketose).

    Quick Review

    • Five types: D/L · pyranose/furanose · α/β anomers · epimers · aldose/ketose.
    • D/L = OH on the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl (C5 in glucose): right → D, left → L. It is configuration, not optical rotation.
    • (+)/(−) is measured with a polarimeter: right = dextrorotatory (+), left = levorotatory (−). D-glucose is D(+); D-fructose is D(−).
    • Pyranose = 6-membered ring (5 C + 1 O); furanose = 5-membered (4 C + 1 O); glucose occurs mainly as pyranose.
    • α: C1 OH down; β: C1 OH up (D-glucose). Anomers differ only at the anomeric carbon.
    • Epimers: galactose = C4 epimer, mannose = C2 epimer of glucose; galactose and mannose differ at two carbons.
    • Glucose = aldose (C1 aldehyde); fructose = ketose (C2 ketone); both C6H12O6.

    Unit 4 of 8

    Glycosides

    Core idea: A glycoside is a sugar part (glycone) joined to a non-sugar part (aglycone) through the sugar’s anomeric carbon.

    5.1 Structure and bonding

    A glycoside consists of a glycone (the sugar part) joined to an aglycone (the non-sugar part) by a glycosidic bond; the sugar links through its anomeric carbon. Thus: glycoside = glycone + aglycone.

    Figure 9 — components of a glycoside 3 parts
    1. GLYCONE — sugar part
    2. Glycosidic bond
    3. AGLYCONE — non-sugar part

    Figure 9. Components of a glycoside. The sugar links through its anomeric carbon.

    • Glycone — usually increases water solubility.
    • Aglycone (genin) — often contributes biological activity. Examples: phenol, steroid, terpene.

    Linkage types are named by the atom attached to the sugar’s anomeric carbon:

    Linkage types 4 rows
    TypeAtom attached to the anomeric carbon
    O-glycosideOxygen
    C-glycosideCarbon
    S-glycosideSulfur
    N-glycosideNitrogen

    5.2 N-linkages and medical examples

    In the N-glycosidic bond of ATP, the sugar’s anomeric carbon bonds to nitrogen in the base: C1′ of ribose is linked to N9 of adenine. ATP (adenosine triphosphate) comprises adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups (associated with Mg2+).

    Figure 10 — N-glycosidic bond in ATP 3 parts
    1. P · P · P three phosphate groups (Mg2+)
    2. Ribose (C1′)
    3. N-glycosidic bond C1′–N9 → Adenine

    Figure 10. Schematic of the N-glycosidic bond in ATP (C1′–N9). ATP = adenosine triphosphate.

    Other glycosides with medical importance. The following are examples of biologically important glycosides, not necessarily N-glycosides:

    • Cardiac glycosides — example: ouabain, which inhibits the Na+/K+-ATPase pump.
    • Antibiotic glycosides — example: streptomycin, an aminoglycoside antibiotic.

    Quick Review

    • Glycoside = glycone (sugar) + aglycone/genin (non-sugar), linked via the anomeric carbon by a glycosidic bond.
    • Glycone usually increases water solubility; aglycone often contributes biological activity (phenol, steroid, terpene).
    • Linkage types: O (oxygen) · C (carbon) · S (sulfur) · N (nitrogen).
    • ATP: ribose C1′ – adenine N9 (N-glycosidic); adenine + ribose + 3 phosphates (with Mg2+).
    • Ouabain (cardiac glycoside) inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase; streptomycin (aminoglycoside antibiotic).

    Unit 5 of 8

    Modified Monosaccharides

    Core idea: Deoxy sugars lose a hydroxyl oxygen; amino sugars have an amino group in place of a hydroxyl group.

    6.1 Deoxy sugars

    In a deoxy sugar, a hydroxyl group (–OH) is replaced by hydrogen (–H), leaving one less oxygen atom at that position. An example is 2-deoxy-D-ribose, the sugar found in DNA (β-D-2-deoxyribofuranose): the missing oxygen is at carbon 2, where H replaces OH. Deoxyribose forms part of the sugar–phosphate backbone of DNA.

    Figure 11. β-D-2-Deoxyribofuranose. At C2, H replaces OH (callout: “C2: H replaces OH”).

    6.2 Amino sugars

    In an amino sugar, an amino group replaces a hydroxyl group (–OH → –NH2); the amino group may be protonated (–NH3+). In D-glucosamine, the amino group is at C2.

    Figure 12. D-Glucosamine, with the amino group at C2 (callout: “Amino group at C2”; shown as NH3+).

    Amino sugars and their importance 3 rows
    Amino sugarImportance
    D-GlucosamineIts N-acetyl derivative is a component of hyaluronic acid.
    D-Galactosamine (chondrosamine)Its N-acetyl derivative is a component of chondroitin sulfate in cartilage.
    ErythromycinContains the amino sugar desosamine.

    Key point. Hexosamines are amino derivatives of six-carbon sugars.

    Quick Review

    • Deoxy sugar: –OH → –H. 2-Deoxy-D-ribose (β-D-2-deoxyribofuranose) is in DNA; H replaces OH at C2.
    • Amino sugar: –OH → –NH2 (may be –NH3+); in D-glucosamine the amino group is at C2.
    • N-acetyl glucosamine → hyaluronic acid; N-acetyl galactosamine (chondrosamine) → chondroitin sulfate in cartilage; erythromycin contains desosamine.
    • Hexosamines = amino derivatives of six-carbon sugars.

    Unit 6 of 8

    Physiologically Important Disaccharides

    Core idea: Disaccharides are two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond; a free anomeric carbon gives reducing properties.

    7. Physiologically Important Disaccharides

    Disaccharides are two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond. A free anomeric carbon gives reducing properties.

    Maltose, lactose, sucrose, lactulose 4 rows
    DisaccharideCompositionLinkage · propertyNotesFull name
    MaltoseGlucose + Glucoseα(1→4) · ReducingFormed during starch breakdown.O-α-D-Glucopyranosyl-(1→4)-α-D-glucopyranose
    LactoseGalactose + Glucoseβ(1→4) · ReducingFound in milk. Lactase deficiency → lactose intolerance.O-β-D-Galactopyranosyl-(1→4)-β-D-glucopyranose
    SucroseGlucose + Fructoseα(1→2)β · Non-reducingFound in cane and beet sugar. Sucrase deficiency → sucrose intolerance.O-α-D-Glucopyranosyl-(1→2)-β-D-fructofuranoside
    LactuloseGalactose + Fructose—Synthetic disaccharide · Used as a laxative.—

    Figure 13. Physiologically important disaccharides (schematic Haworth structures; the glycosidic oxygen links the two rings).

    Key point. A free anomeric carbon gives reducing properties.

    Quick Review

    • Maltose = Glc + Glc, α(1→4), reducing (from starch breakdown).
    • Lactose = Gal + Glc, β(1→4), reducing (milk); lactase deficiency → lactose intolerance.
    • Sucrose = Glc + Fru, α(1→2)β, non-reducing (cane/beet sugar); sucrase deficiency → sucrose intolerance.
    • Lactulose = Gal + Fru, synthetic, laxative.

    Unit 7 of 8

    Polysaccharides: Storage and Structure

    Core idea: Starch and glycogen store glucose; inulin and cellulose are plant polysaccharides that human digestive enzymes cannot break down.

    8.1 Overview

    • Starch represents a homopolymer of glucose units forming a highly regulated α-glucosidic chain called glucosan. It is the single most vital calorie source across standard diets (found in potatoes, cereals, and legumes). It splits into two sub-structures:
      1. Amylose (13–20%): features a fully continuous, non-branching, tight helical coil structure.
      2. Amylopectin (80–85%): consists of branched chains spanning 24 to 30 glucose blocks linked via α(1→4) bonds inside core lines, and α(1→6) bonds at branch points.
    • Glycogen: often classified as “animal starch”, glycogen acts as the primary systemic carbohydrate reservoir inside animals.

    8.2 Starch

    Starch is a plant storage polysaccharide made of glucose units and is a major dietary carbohydrate (potatoes, cereals and legumes). It contains both amylose and amylopectin.

    Starch components 2 rows
    ComponentProportion*Structure and bonds
    AmyloseAbout 13–20%Unbranched, helical chain; α(1→4) glycosidic bonds.
    AmylopectinAbout 80–85%Branched glucose chains; branches about every 24–30 glucose units.

    *Typical proportions; vary with the plant source.

    Figure 14. Starch components (simplified structures; H and OH groups omitted). Amylose: α(1→4) glycosidic bonds; unbranched, helical chain; about 13–20%*. Amylopectin: α(1→6) branch; branched glucose chains; branches about every 24–30 glucose units; about 80–85%*. *Typical proportions; they vary with the plant source.

    Key point. Starch contains both amylose and amylopectin.

    8.3 Glycogen

    Glycogen is the main storage polysaccharide in animals and is often called “animal starch”.

    Glycogen features 4 rows
    FeatureDescription
    Building blockα-D-glucopyranose (glucose)
    Chain lengthAbout 12–14 glucose residues
    BranchingMore highly branched than amylopectin
    Storage sitesStored mainly in liver and skeletal muscle

    Figure 15. Glycogen: simplified schematic; each circle represents glucose. Legend: glucose residue, α(1→4) in chains; branch point, α(1→6).

    Key takeaway. Glucose chains: α(1→4) · Branch points: α(1→6).

    8.4 Inulin and cellulose

    Inulin and cellulose are plant polysaccharides that human digestive enzymes cannot break down.

    Inulin vs cellulose 4 rows
    InulinCellulose
    CompositionFructose polymer.β-D-glucose units joined by β(1→4) bonds; hydrogen bonds between chains.
    OccurrenceFound in roots and tubers of selected plants.Main structural component of plant cell walls.
    DigestionNot digested by human enzymes.Insoluble dietary fiber. Humans lack cellulase → cellulose adds bulk to stool.
    Clinical useInulin clearance measures GFR (glomerular filtration rate).—

    Figure 16. Inulin (fructose polymer) and cellulose (glucose polymer; simplified chain schematic). Inulin = fructose units. Cellulose: dashed lines = hydrogen bonds between chains.

    Microbial fermentation. Gut microbes can break down some fiber into short-chain fatty acids. Cellulose fermentation is extensive in ruminants and more limited in humans.

    Key point. Inulin = fructose polymer · Cellulose = glucose polymer.

    Quick Review

    • Starch (plant glucose homopolymer, “glucosan”): amylose 13–20% (unbranched helix, α(1→4)) + amylopectin 80–85% (branches every 24–30 glucose units, α(1→6) at branch points).
    • Glycogen (“animal starch”): glucose chains of about 12–14 residues, more branched than amylopectin; stored in liver and skeletal muscle.
    • Chains α(1→4) · branch points α(1→6).
    • Inulin = fructose polymer (inulin clearance measures GFR). Cellulose = β(1→4) glucose polymer, insoluble fiber, humans lack cellulase.

    Unit 8 of 8

    Complex Carbohydrates

    Core idea: Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are long chains of repeating disaccharides; glycoproteins are proteins carrying oligosaccharide chains.

    9.1 Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs; mucopolysaccharides)

    GAGs are long sugar chains made of repeating disaccharides.

    • Composition: usually an amino sugar + a uronic acid.
    • With protein: GAG chains + core protein → proteoglycan. Exception: hyaluronic acid is not covalently attached to a core protein.
    • Main role: negative charges attract water, forming a hydrated gel in the extracellular matrix.
    • Functions: cushioning, lubrication and filling space.
    Table 2 — Examples of glycosaminoglycans 3 rows
    GAGRepeating sugar componentsSulfation
    Hyaluronic acidGlucuronic acid + N-acetylglucosamineUnsulfated
    Chondroitin sulfateGlucuronic acid + N-acetylgalactosamineSulfated
    HeparinGlucosamine + uronic acid (often iduronic acid)Highly sulfated

    9.2 Glycoproteins

    Glycoproteins are proteins with covalently attached oligosaccharide chains (older term: mucoproteins).

    • Structure: protein + short carbohydrate chains; the chains may be branched or unbranched.
    • Sugar examples: mannose, galactose, arabinose and xylose. Arabinose is especially associated with plant glycoproteins.
    • Where found: cell membranes, and blood serum (examples: transferrin and immunoglobulins).

    Key takeaway. Glycoprotein = protein + oligosaccharide chains.

    Quick Review

    • GAGs: repeating disaccharides, usually amino sugar + uronic acid; GAG + core protein → proteoglycan (exception: hyaluronic acid).
    • Negative charges attract water → hydrated gel in extracellular matrix; cushioning, lubrication, filling space.
    • Hyaluronic acid: glucuronic acid + N-acetylglucosamine, unsulfated · Chondroitin sulfate: glucuronic acid + N-acetylgalactosamine, sulfated · Heparin: glucosamine + uronic acid (often iduronic), highly sulfated.
    • Glycoprotein = protein + oligosaccharide chains (cell membranes, serum: transferrin, immunoglobulins).

    Figure 15 · Section 7.2

    Tap a highlighted part

    D-Glucosamine, with the amino group at C2.

    Key point. Amino sugar: –NH₂ (or –NH₃⁺) replaces OH at C2. Hexosamines are amino derivatives of six-carbon sugars.

    Maltose, Lactose and Sucrose

    Disaccharides

    Figure 16 · Section 8

    Tap a highlighted part

    Physiologically important disaccharides (schematic Haworth structures; the glycosidic oxygen links the two rings).

    Key point. A free anomeric carbon gives reducing properties: maltose α(1→4) and lactose β(1→4) are reducing; sucrose α(1→2)β is non-reducing.

    Starch: Amylose and Amylopectin

    Polysaccharides

    Figure 17 · Section 9.2

    Tap a highlighted part

    Starch components (simplified structures; H and OH groups omitted). *Typical proportions; they vary with the plant source.

    Key point. Amylose: unbranched helix, α(1→4). Amylopectin: branched, α(1→6) every 24–30 glucose units.

    Figure 18 · Section 9.3

    Glycogen: simplified schematic; each circle represents glucose.

    Key point. Chains α(1→4) · branch points α(1→6). More highly branched than amylopectin (chains of ~12–14 residues).
